title: Quantum simulation of material-specific Hubbard models with alkaline-earth atoms
authors: Henning Schlömer, Reuben R. W. Wang, Bo Xing, Susanne F. Yelin, H. R. Sadeghpour
abstract: A long-term goal of quantum simulation is to faithfully reproduce the low-energy Hamiltonians of correlated quantum materials, establishing a direct connection between solid-state experiment, electronic-structure theory, and programmable many-body systems. Here, we introduce an integrated quantum-simulation architecture based on fermionic alkaline-earth atoms that enables programmable control over the key ingredients of multi-orbital material Hamiltonians. Long-lived clock states encode synthetic orbitals, their differential polarizabilities generate orbital-selective tunneling, and contact interactions provide multi-orbital Hubbard and Hund couplings. Spatially structured coherent driving on the ultra-narrow clock transition further realizes symmetry-selective inter-orbital hybridization, while the clock detuning independently controls orbital energy offsets. In this way, the spatial symmetries of solid-state orbitals can be encoded directly into the effective Hamiltonian, even though the atoms themselves remain in conventional $s$-wave Wannier orbitals of the lowest optical-lattice bands. We demonstrate the resulting integrated control using the four-band low-energy Hamiltonian of the bilayer nickelate La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ as a demanding benchmark. Self-consistent calculations show that the microscopic parameters obtained from first-principles modeling can be reproduced within a single experimentally accessible lattice configuration and independently programmed over substantial parameter ranges. Our results establish a general route for translating material-derived multi-orbital Hamiltonians into programmable ultracold-atom quantum simulators.
summary: This paper introduces a comprehensive quantum simulation architecture using alkaline-earth atoms to model the complex, multi-orbital physics found in correlated materials like nickelates. By combining various laser and lattice controls, the authors achieve programmable control over all necessary Hamiltonian terms, demonstrating a general route to simulate solid-state physics in an ultracold atom setting.
main_problem: The goal is to faithfully reproduce the complex, multi-orbital Hamiltonians of correlated quantum materials, such as bilayer nickelates, using programmable quantum simulators.
main_result: The authors demonstrate an integrated architecture using fermionic alkaline-earth atoms that can programmatically control all necessary ingredients—including orbital-selective tunneling, multi-orbital Hubbard/Hund couplings, and crystal field splitting—to simulate these complex models.
method: The approach combines advanced atomic physics techniques (clock states, structured driving, Feshbach resonances) to engineer the effective Hamiltonian, which is then benchmarked against first-principles calculations from solid-state theory.
model_or_system: The system uses fermionic alkaline-earth atoms in an optical lattice to simulate the low-energy physics of correlated materials, specifically targeting the four-band Hamiltonian of bilayer nickelates. The simulation controls hopping hierarchies, interaction strengths ($U, J_H, V$), and orbital energy offsets independently.
key_observables: Non-interacting band structure (e.g., $\alpha,  eta, \gamma$ pockets), orbital-dependent hopping ratios, and the ability to reproduce microscopic parameters from first-principles modeling.
important_parameters: The simulation requires independent control over hopping ratios ($t_{\parallel}/t_{\perp}$), interaction strengths ($U, J_H, V$), and crystal field splitting ($\Delta$).
main_assumptions: The method successfully encodes solid-state orbital symmetries into the effective Hamiltonian even when atoms are confined to simple $s$-wave Wannier orbitals. The realization requires a demanding combination of laser and lattice control.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the 'Toolbox' for simulation, mapping material requirements to atomic controls, and detail the specific hopping hierarchies and level schemes required to model the bilayer nickelate structure.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the general goal of simulating material Hamiltonians, details the specific physical ingredients (orbital encoding, coupling, detuning) available in the AEA platform, and validates this capability by applying it to the highly demanding benchmark of the bilayer nickelate model.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, general blueprint for realizing complex, multi-orbital Hamiltonians in ultracold atoms, bridging the gap between high-level condensed matter theory and programmable quantum hardware.
